power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_exact.title: Exact P-Values
stat_p_exact.summary_text: We found 1 imprecise *p* value out of 7 detected *p* values.

table.formatted: Substantial postoperative increases were observed for most CSF biomarkers: The largest relative increases were seen for growth-associated protein 43 (GAP43) (2.92-fold change), followed by Phosphorylated tau (2.65-fold change), Neurogranin and total-tau (both 2.29-fold change) as well as Aβ40 (1.93-fold change), and Aβ42 (1.76-fold change) (all p<0.001).
table.expanded: Substantial postoperative increases were observed for most CSF biomarkers: The largest relative increases were seen for growth-associated protein 43 (GAP43) (2.92-fold change), followed by Phosphorylated tau (2.65-fold change), Neurogranin and total-tau (both 2.29-fold change) as well as Aβ40 (1.93-fold change), and Aβ42 (1.76-fold change) (all p<0.001).

table.formatted: The mean iNPH total score increased from 53.8 to 66.2 points (p<0.001).
table.expanded: The mean iNPH total score increased from 53.8 to 66.2 points (p<0.001).

table.formatted: All tested biomarkers increased significantly after surgery, with the largest relative increase observed for GAP43 (2.92-fold change), followed by P-tau (2.65-fold change), NG and T-tau (both 2.29-fold change) as well as Aβ40 (1.93-fold change), and Aβ42 (1.76-fold change) (all p<0.001).
table.header: Changes in CSF biomarker concentrations following shunt surgery
table.expanded: All tested biomarkers increased significantly after surgery, with the largest relative increase observed for GAP43 (2.92-fold change), followed by P-tau (2.65-fold change), NG and T-tau (both 2.29-fold change) as well as Aβ40 (1.93-fold change), and Aβ42 (1.76-fold change) (all p<0.001).

table.formatted: In adjusted analyses, increases in GFAP, YKL40, and GAP43 were associated with greater improvement in the total iNPH scale score (partial r=0.20-0.28; all p<0.05).
table.header: Associations between biomarker changes and clinical improvement
table.expanded: In adjusted analyses, increases in GFAP, YKL40, and GAP43 were associated with greater improvement in the total iNPH scale score (partial r=0.20-0.28; all p<0.05).

MCP1 was the only biomarker significantly associated with improvement in the total iNPH scale score, with lower baseline levels associated with greater odds of clinical improvement (adjusted OR 0.45, 95% CI 0.24-0.85; p=0.014).
Lower baseline levels of Aβ40 (Adjusted OR 0.63, 95% CI 0.40-0.99; p=0.047), and Aβ42 (Adjusted OR 0.54, 95% CI 0.35-0.83; p=0.005) were associated with less postoperative urinary incontinence.
Lower baseline levels of Aβ40 (Adjusted OR 0.63, 95% CI 0.40-0.99; p=0.047), and Aβ42 (Adjusted OR 0.54, 95% CI 0.35-0.83; p=0.005) were associated with less postoperative urinary incontinence.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p<0.05", Text = "In adjusted analyses, increases in GFAP, YKL40, and GAP43 were associated with greater improvement in the total iNPH scale score (partial r=0.20-0.28; all p<0.05)."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::
